articles.title: No allocentric distractor-location learning following self-movement even with contextual anchors and explicit knowledge
articles.content: Adaptive behavior requires learning where relevant information can likely be found, but also where distraction is likely to occur. For such learning to be useful in everyday life, it must generalize across changing viewpoints as observers move through the environment. Recent work suggests a striking asymmetry in this regard: whereas target-location learning can be grounded in world-centered coordinates, distractor-location learning appears tied to the observer's current viewpoint. One possibility is that allocentric distractor-location learning requires stronger contextual support than allocentric target-location learning. Alternatively, distractor suppression may be fundamentally constrained by viewer-centered spatial coding. To distinguish between these possibilities, participants performed an additional-singleton search task displayed on a tabletop and continuously changed their standing position around the table, while the high-probability distractor location remained fixed in the external environment. Unlike previous studies using this paradigm, contextual anchors were embedded directly within the search display, allowing distractor locations to be encoded relative to a stable task-relevant allocentric structure. In a second experiment, participants were additionally explicitly informed about the distractor-location regularity. Despite task-relevant contextual structure and explicit knowledge, distractor-location learning failed to emerge in world-centered coordinates. Together with previous findings showing robust egocentric distractor-location learning using the same set-up, these findings strengthen the view that learned distractor suppression relies primarily on viewer-centered spatial coding, potentially reflecting a process linked to viewpoint-specific action selection.
articles.author: Chen, L., Fatato, C., Jia, S., van Ede, F., Slagter, H. A.

articles.title: ACC Sulcal Morphology as a Neurodevelopmental Marker of Proactive and Reactive Cognitive Control among Adolescents
articles.content: Behavioral inhibition (BI) is an early temperament associated with higher risk for later anxiety. BI has been linked to variation in cognitive control, particularly proactive control, a crucial component of executive functions which involves monitoring one's own behavior and adapting that behavior to achieve a particular goal, which may help explain BI's association with elevated anxiety risk. Yet little is known about the neurobiology of cognitive control development among children with BI. Variation in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) sulcal pattern asymmetry, established prenatally and stable across development, is associated with individual differences in cognitive control. This preliminary study examined whether ACC sulcal symmetry is associated with BI, proactive and reactive control (measured via the AX-CPT) in adolescents. Structural T1-weighted MRI was acquired from 62 adolescents aged 12 to 15 years. ACC patterns in each hemisphere were classified as 'single type' or 'double parallel type' based on the presence of a paracingulate sulcus. Adolescents with symmetric ACC patterns showed lower proactive control (d' context; 2p = .091) and greater reactive control (BX probe interference effect; 2p = .119). These associations held even when tested within the same statistical model and were comparable in magnitude. ACC symmetry was not associated with BI, nor did it interact with BI to predict cognitive control scores. Overall, the findings provide preliminary evidence that ACC sulcal morphology may be a structural marker of variability in cognitive control, with relevance to BI-related neurocognitive risk.
articles.author: Lassaigne, M., Cachia, A., Pine, D. S., Fox, N. A., Valadez, E. A.

articles.title: Intra-thalamic coordination maintains arousability in slow-wave sleep
articles.content: Slow-wave sleep preserves the capacity for spontaneous or stimulus-evoked awakening despite reduced responsiveness, yet how thalamic nuclei coordinate to preserve arousability remains unclear. We analysed six fMRI and EEG datasets spanning sleep, propofol anesthesia and unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (UWS). During N2 and N3, centromedian (CM) and ventral posterolateral (VPL) nuclei showed convergent edge-community profiles and increased closed-loop intra-thalamic motifs, changes not observed during anesthesia or UWS. During N3, directed effective connectivity along CM[->]VPL[->]pulvinar (PUL) increased versus wakefulness and N2. Stronger CM[->]VPL and VPL[->]PUL connectivity covaried with greater N3 delta power, which was higher before awakening than before transitions to N2 and positively associated with three-month improvement in behavioural responsiveness in UWS. These findings identify a CM-VPL-PUL-centred pattern of intra-thalamic organization linked to preserved arousability during slow-wave sleep, extending accounts focused on individual nuclei and thalamocortical interactions.
articles.author: Han, J., Xie, Q., Huang, Y., Li, M., Hu, X., Northoff, G., Li, Y., Zhang, J., Qin, P.

articles.title: Cross-species phosphoproteomic mapping of mTORC1 signalling reveals RNA splicing regulation during neurodevelopment
articles.content: Mechanistic target of rapamycin complex 1 (mTORC1) regulates diverse cellular processes through its kinase activity and is essential for nervous system development. Although mTORC1 hyperactivation causes numerous neurodevelopmental disorders, its downstream targets in the developing nervous system remain poorly defined. Here, by profiling thousands of proteins and tens of thousands of phosphosites during the neurogenic phase in mouse and human models, we systematically define the proteomic and phosphoproteomic landscape downstream of mTORC1 during neurodevelopment. To facilitate community access, we developed PhosphoTargets, an interactive platform comprising protein and phosphoprotein expression data from mTORC1 models and patient tissue. We demonstrate the utility of this resource by identifying the deubiquitylating enzyme USP9X as a novel mTORC1 substrate and showing that mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation of USP9X regulates human neural progenitor cell proliferation. Furthermore, integration with gene expression datasets reveals a new role for mTORC1 in the regulation of mRNA splicing. Together, these data provide a comprehensive resource for investigating mTORC1 signalling mechanisms and reveal novel processes through which mTORC1 regulates neurodevelopment.

articles.title: Context-dependent requirement for neutrophils in retinal regeneration
articles.content: Innate immune responses shape Muller glia (MG) reprogramming and retinal regeneration, yet the contribution of individual immune cell type remains poorly defined. Neutrophils enter the blood-retinal-barrier (BRB)-damaged retina within hours of injury, but their role in retinal regeneration is unknown. Here we report that neutrophils are required for the regenerative responses in needle-poked, but not NMDA-injured, zebrafish retinas. Pharmacological ablation of neutrophils with Erbb2 inhibitors suppresses MG proliferation, progenitor formation, and subsequent neuronal regeneration after stab injury, whereas neutrophil depletion has no significant effect in the BRB-intact NMDA model. We further show that Cxcl12-Cxcr4b signaling retains neutrophils at the stab injury site, and manipulating neutrophil retention correspondingly alters the regenerative responses. Mechanistically, neutrophils may modulate MG reprogramming and proliferation by regulating microglial reactivity and by secreting a regeneration-promoting factor Hb-egf. These data identify neutrophil as a previously unrecognized regulator of retinal regeneration and establish that their contribution is injury context-dependent.
articles.author: Li, Y., Xu, T., Zhi, Y., Zhao, R., Lu, Q., Xu, H.

articles.title: A temporal atlas of TDP-43 interactions reveals persistent network remodelling beyond stress granule clearance
articles.content: Cytoplasmic aggregation of the nuclear protein TDP-43 is associated with several neurodegenerative disorders and may be promoted by cellular stress. However, the dynamics of TDP-43 protein-protein interactions during stress and recovery remain poorly understood. Here, we combined APEX2 proximity labelling with quantitative mass spectrometry to generate a temporal atlas of wild-type TDP-43 and pathology-mimicking TDP-43dNLS and TDP-43CTF variants. Interactomes were profiled across steady state, oxidative stress, and recovery. We reveal extensive state- and variant-dependent remodelling of TDP-43 interaction networks, uncovering distinct temporal interaction patterns throughout the stress response and recovery. Notably, distinct TDP-43 interaction signatures persisted after stress granule clearance, suggesting a molecular memory of stress. Together, our study establishes a comprehensive temporal resource for investigating TDP-43 interaction dynamics and provides a framework for understanding how stress-induced network alterations may contribute to TDP-43 proteinopathies.

articles.title: Neural reactivation of past events tracks narrative understanding as it unfolds
articles.content: Understanding of episodic experience is not achieved at a single moment: it is a constructive process in which each new event is interpreted in light of relevant past events and prior knowledge. Yet this process is rarely measured as it unfolds, leaving unclear how the brain integrates past events to construct an evolving understanding of the present. We hypothesized that neural reactivation of past events at narrative event boundaries reflects not merely what people experience, but how they interpret their experience. We developed a behavioural paradigm that tracks, as a narrative unfolds, which past events people consider relevant for understanding each new event. By manipulating prior knowledge of the narrative's final plot twist, we examined the process by which the same experience yields different understanding. Across independent behavioural and fMRI cohorts, we found that prior knowledge similarly altered the variability and intersubject similarity of inferred relations between events and their neural reactivation at narrative event boundaries in the Default Mode Network. Moreover, stronger neural reactivation was associated with greater inferred relevance between events, and event pairs showing different behavioural relations across groups also showed corresponding differences in reactivation. These findings suggest that neural reactivation of past events at event boundaries reflects an unfolding inferential process that transforms shared experience into subjective understanding.
articles.author: Chan, K. Y. I., Mouloudi, I., Ben-Yakov, A., Dubossarsky, H., Hahamy, A.

articles.title: Genetic, neural and early-environmental architecture of resilience
articles.content: Resilience is shaped by factors ranging from the genome through early-life experience to the brain, yet its biological basis in humans remains unclear because studies have rarely integrated these levels and have been confined to small samples. Using the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS) and multimodal data from tens of thousands of UK Biobank (UKB) participants, with replication in Generation Scotland (GS), we found that resting-state functional connectivity, particularly within the flexibility and valuation networks, is a robust neural correlate of resilience. Resilience also showed a generalizable genetic basis: a polygenic score (PGS) derived from a UKB genome-wide association study predicted BRS in GS. Genes and childhood experiences converged on the flexibility network through distinct routes: the polygenic association with resilience was partly explained by central executive-salience integration, whereas childhood experiences were associated with default-mode-centered integration. By separating genetically anchored from experience-sensitive routes, these findings point to network targets that interventions could tailor to the sources of an individual's vulnerability.
articles.author: Wu, T.-Y., Yang, Y.-Y., Liang, Y.-J., Lin, F.-H., Yang, H.-C., Huang, C.-Y.

articles.title: A radial glial regulatory program bridges progenitor maintenance and neuronal identity
articles.content: The cerebral cortex acquires its neuronal diversity through successive waves of neurogenesis. How molecular differences among early progenitors relate to their neuronal output remains unclear. Here, we identify a molecular program in early SOX9-high radial glia (S9RGs) that links progenitor maintenance with the regulation of genes associated with neuronal identity. Combining transcriptional and chromatin profiling with in vivo perturbations, we identify a program involving extracellular signaling, cell-cycle regulation, progenitor maintenance, and neurogenesis. We show that SOX9 regulates part of this program, including receptors that contribute to progenitor maintenance, while Notch acts upstream of Sox9 and reproduces several transcriptional and chromatin features of S9RGs. S9RGs express selected later-stage radial glial features and show distinct chromatin accessibility patterns at genes involved in progenitor maintenance, neurogenesis, and neuronal identity. Notch activation reproduces part of these changes, including differences at genes associated with lower- and upper-layer neuronal specification. Interestingly, S9RGs, which preferentially generate upper-layer neurons, share molecular features with the highly proliferative RG population in ferrets and with human outer RGs (oRGs) from cortical organoids, despite their different positions within the developing cortex. Together, our findings suggest that molecular differences among early radial glia could influence both how long they remain as progenitors and the neuronal identities they subsequently generate.
articles.author: Fabra-Beser, J., Planells, J., Tran, L. L., Turskan, D., Marin-Garnes, A., Veintimilla-Escot, L., Mateos-Martinez, C. M., Gibson, T. J., Franco, S. J., Gil-Sanz, C.

articles.title: Gene expression in the hypothalamus of gonad-sex chromosome divergent embryonic chickens
articles.content: Sexual differentiation of the brain of birds is shaped by gonadal steroid hormones and also by cell-autonomous mechanisms resulting from limited sex chromosome dosage compensation. In this study, we compare gene expression in the hypothalamus of gonad-sex chromosome divergent embryonic chickens treated with the aromatase inhibitor fadrozole to their control counterparts. Consistent with a lack of dosage compensation, we find a robust effect of sex chromosomes on hypothalamic gene expression, and a large portion of differentially expressed genes were on the Z and W sex chromosomes. Despite the presence of developing testes and markedly reduced estrogen concentrations in fadrozole-treated chromosomal female (ZW) birds, we find modest effects of gonadal hormones on gene expression in the brain. Weighted gene coexpression network analysis revealed that the most prominent effects were attributable to interactions between chromosomal sex and treatment. Our results highlight that chromosomal sex and steroid hormones together shape the sexual differentiation of the embryonic avian brain, challenging the primacy of the organizational effects of sex steroids on the brain during development.

articles.title: When neuroscience meets machine learning: a taxonomic scoping review of machine and statistical learning approaches in sub-Saharan Africa
articles.content: In high-resource economies, computational neuroscience research frequently employs machine learning (ML) and statistical learning (SL) techniques. While these methods provide effective ways to analyse multimodal, high-dimensional, and complex data they are underexplored in low resource settings. This taxonomic scoping review uses a systematic methodological approach to synthesise the application of ML and SL techniques in neuroscience research in sub-Saharan Africa. In addition to discussing findings, strengths, limitations, and future prospects, the work classifies current research by neuroscience domains, applications, learning tasks, datasets, tools, and techniques. In order for African researchers to contribute to and benefit from the global computational neuroscience landscape, our review contends that low- and middle-income countries must create and augment context-specific and representative datasets and incorporate appropriate features for model training. Future studies should focus on pragmatic rather than complex modelling, external validation, reproducibility, interpretability, and utilise real-world data to determine clinical utility.
articles.author: Deshendran Moodley

articles.title: Validation of the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised in patients with disorders of consciousness
articles.content: ObjectiveOur objective was to validate the Hungarian version of the Coma Recovery Scale-Revised (CRS-R).DesignWe conducted a multicenter study across neurology, intensive care, neuro-rehabilitation, and nursing departments in Hungary. Thirty-one patients (17 males; mean age 49.1 ± 16.1 years) with disorders of consciousness (DOC) following severe acquired brain injury were assessed. Two independent raters reassessed the same patients within a one-week window to evaluate inter-rater and intra-rater reliability. We assessed reliability using weighted Cohen’s Kappa and evaluated concurrent validity using Spearman’s rank correlation.ResultsConcurrent validity with the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was strong across all raters and time points (rho = 0.882–0.934, p < 0.001). Inter-rater reliability for the total score was excellent at initial assessment (wk = 0.977) and remained high at follow-up (wk = 0.977). Diagnostic classification agreement between raters was nearly perfect (wk = 0.936–1.000).ConclusionThe Hungarian CRS-R is a valid and reliable instrument that preserves the robustness of the original version. Its implementation fills a critical gap in national healthcare by providing an evidence-based tool to reduce DOC misdiagnosis rates.
